new_statements.quote: From my data, at the current stage of analysis, I do not have any reason for assuming word stress in Yali. However, Yali does have a rather regularly word-final pitch rise, creating a salient rhythmic structure in its utterances. [...] Secondly, the word-final pitch movement is not lexically contrastive, but occurs completely regularly with just any (type of) word. Thirdly, and perhaps most importantly, its domain can sometimes be larger than a phonological word [...]. In total, therefore, I describe this pitch rise as an edge tone marking the right boundary of the AP in Yali, a mostly word-sized constituent that can sometimes also be larger, but never smaller than the phonological word

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: verbatim at Gayler 2025 sec. 2.4.1 'Word stress in Yali?', printed p. 53 = p. 61 of (extracted text). All three quoted stretches match word for word; the '[..]' elisions correctly drop the Bromley/Burung comparison and 'i.e. not really every phonological word actually has the final rise'; the last sentence ends '(cf. section 2.2)' in the original. The Kaland et al. 2026 p. 21 passages ('it seems unlikely that Yali has stressed syllables'; 'tentatively categorised as a non-stress-accent language with only post-lexical pitch'; 'more plausible that Yali has a word-level (pitch) accent system rather than word stress'; 'it remains a question for future research whether word stress is inde…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word stress is posited. Every content word (phonological word) ends in a low-high pitch rise on its final syllable; this is analysed as a (L+)H edge tone marking the right edge of the accentual phrase, which is usually one phonological word but can be larger, never smaller. The rise is non-contrastive, shifts onto suffixes but not onto free grammatical words, can reduce to a level H on short/function words, and is replaced by a low boundary tone (fall) at the end of a finality-marking intonation unit. The instrumental companion (Kaland et al. 2026 p. 21) finds no duration difference between word-final and non-final syllables and tentatively classes Yali as a non-stress-accent language with post-lexical pitch only, i.e. a word-level (pitch) accent system rather than stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (no stress at all is posited).
new_statements.exceptions: Both sources are explicitly tentative ('at the current stage of analysis'; 'it remains a question for future research whether word stress is indeed absent'). The rise can be reduced to a level H on short/function words; not every phonological word carries it when the accentual phrase spans more than one word; IU-final falling contour overrides it. Gayler's prosodic description is based on auditory/visual inspection, not measurement (p. 27); Kaland et al. supply the acoustic evidence. Neighbouring Dani languages (Lower Grand Valley Dani, Wano, Western Dani) are described with final word stress, Nggem with penultimate; both sources argue that those 'stress' claims may correspond to the same word-final pitch event.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word / accentual phrase in connected spontaneous speech (narrative corpus and elicited sentences); the word-final rise is an edge tone of the accentual phrase, not a lexical property; phrase-level boundary tones override it. Not citation forms.
new_statements.first_reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (and the instrumental companion Kaland et al. 2026) describes Apahapsili Yali, the dialect that Glottolog files under Pass Valley Yali (pass1247, ISO yac), not Ninia Yali (nini1235, nlk). No phonological description of Ninia Yali itself exists (Glottolog: zero descriptive refs; Riesberg 2021 p. 2 names only Wilson 1988, a theological/ethnographic thesis). Riesberg 2021 p. 1 and Gayler 2025 pp. 18-19 state that the three Glottolog Yalic languages are mutually intelligible and that differences are 'mostly lexical or phonological'; the reviewer must decide whether the Apahapsili finding may stand in for Ninia or should be filed under pass1247 instead. The Riesberg sketch (silent on stress) describes Angguruk Yali (angg1239, yli).
